# Row-Oriented and Columnar Data

| Layout Type| Definition | Best For | File Type |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Row-Oriented | Data sits in one continuous block on disk | Transactional systems (OLTP) | CSV, JSON, Traditional SQL |
| Columnar | All values for a single column are grouped together sequentially on disk | Analytical querying (OLAP) and Data Warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery) | Parquet, ORC (Optimized Row Columnar) |

Row-Oriented **Disadvantage**: massive disk I/O bottlenecks when reading unnecessary columns because row-based block storage.

Columnar Data **Advantage**: **Heavy Compression** because a single column shares the exact same data type (e.g., all integers or all strings).

## Difference Between Parquet and ORC

Parquet and ORC are both columnar storage formats, but Parquet excels in read-heavy analytical workloads while ORC is optimized for write-heavy tasks and Hive integration.

## Apache Parquet **Projection Pushdown**

Definition: when your pipeline requests specific columns, the file reader reads the file's footer metadata first, maps exactly where those columns are physically located on disk, and extracts only those bytes. The technique reads only the specific columns requested in a query. By "pushing" the column selection down to the storage layer, the query engine skips parsing or retrieving irrelevant data, drastically reducing disk I/O and network transfers.

::: {.callout-note}
There is also another technique called **Predicate Pushdown**, which is optimised to reduce rows (rather than columns). This is covered in [Week4 Day 5 study](https://awesomeyi-blog.share.connect.posit.cloud/advance-python-skill/WK4D5/).
:::

### Why Projection Pushdown matters financially?

In production, when querying terabytes of cloud storage (like AWS S3), **Projection Pushdown** is what prevents your cloud bill from skyrocketing and keeps your pipelines running in seconds rather than hours.

# Sample

```
import pandas as pd

# The Aggressive Row Approach (CSV)
# Even if you look at one column, the engine must parse the entire string file.
df_csv = pd.read_csv("massive_data.csv")
average_balance = df_csv["Account_Balance"].mean()

# The Columnar Approach (Parquet)
# The engine performs Projection Pushdown, only reading the requested column from disk.
df_parquet = pd.read_parquet("massive_data.parquet", columns=["Account_Balance"])
average_balance = df_parquet["Account_Balance"].mean()
```

# Basic usage of the `pyarrow` package

```
# Load pyarrow package
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

# create a table
table = pa.table({"use_id" : [1, 2, 3]}) # this is similar to pd.DataFrame({})

# creat a table from a dictionary
table = pa.Table.from_pydict(data) 

# read a pandas data frame into a Arrow table
table = pa.Table.from_pandas(df)

# export data to a parquet file
pd.write_table(table, "analytics_stream.parquet)

# use projection pushdown to read specific columns
specific_columns = pq.read_table("analytics_stream.parquet", columns=["user_id"])

# export to a pandas data frame
df = pq.read_table("data.parquet").to_pandas()

# read parquet file metadata
parquet_file = pq.ParquetFile("analytics_stream.parquet")
parquet_file.schema
parquet_file.metadata
parquet_file.num_row_groups
```
